tweets.text: $SOFI is expanding its private markets offering with three new funds: CAZ GP Stakes Fund CAZ Strategic Opportunities Fund AngelList USVC Venture Capital Access Fund The funds provide indirect exposure to companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Anduril. Minimum investment is $500 for the USVC fund and $2,500 for the CAZ funds. They’re not fully liquid, but they’re not locked up like traditional private equity either—there will be periodic redemption windows. The interesting part isn’t the product launch itself. SoFi is trying to evolve from a lending company into a financial distribution platform. Over the past year they’ve added products from ARK, KKR, Carlyle, Cashmere, Liberty Street, and Templum. They already have 15.8M members, and 51% of new products are opened by existing members. These funds probably won’t move revenue much on their own, but they can improve engagement and create more cross-selling opportunities. The numbers support that story to some extent. Fee-based revenue reached $472M in Q2, or 39% of total revenue, while brokerage revenue grew 2.5x YoY. That said, the bigger picture hasn’t changed yet. Net interest income was still $788M, growing 52% YoY, so SoFi remains primarily a balance-sheet business. And its most asset-light segment, the Technology Platform, actually declined 23% YoY. The platform strategy is moving in the right direction, but it’s not the core of the business yet. There’s also the investor angle. These are higher-fee, less liquid, and less transparent assets, offered on a self-directed basis. Getting access to private companies like OpenAI sounds exciting—but knowing what valuation you’re buying into is a different question. I like the direction, but I think it’s still too early to say SoFi is no longer a lending company. The metrics I’ll be watching are simple: the share of revenue coming from fees, and whether the Technology Platform returns to growth.

$DDOG Q2 Revenue: $1.12B (+36% YoY) vs. $1.08B expected EPS: $0.65 vs. $0.58 expected FCF: $279M 100K+ ARR customers: 4,720 (+23%) Billings: $1.18B (+38%) The company raised its full-year revenue guidance from $4.32B to $4.46B. Every major metric beat expectations. Yet the stock fell 17%. The issue wasn’t the numbers—it was the trajectory. This quarter’s revenue grew 36%, but Q3 guidance points to roughly 29% growth. Quarterly additions of 100K+ ARR customers slowed to 170, down from the previous quarter. FCF margin also declined from 28.7% to 24.9%. The market has been valuing Datadog largely as an AI story. Its biggest customer in that narrative is OpenAI, and the possibility of OpenAI building more of its own observability infrastructure remains an overhang. At this valuation, simply beating estimates isn’t enough. Investors expect growth to keep accelerating. The company executed well. The bar was just set exceptionally high.

$ASTS has begun integration testing across eight countries in Europe. Working alongside Vodafone, Orange, Telefónica, Deutsche Telekom, and Vodafone Ukraine, the company is using standard smartphones and a shared gateway infrastructure to bring direct-to-smartphone satellite connectivity one step closer to commercial launch. This progress with major European mobile operators is accelerating the company’s global expansion. A strong and significant milestone.

$OSCR Oscar Health Q2’26 Revenue: $4.88B (+70% YoY) Net income: $361.8M (vs. $228.4M loss last year) Diluted EPS: $1.10 Adj. EBITDA: $415.3M Members: 2.96M (+46%) MLR: 79.2% (vs. 91.1% last year) SG&A ratio: 14.2% The headline numbers are strong, but two details matter. The improvement in MLR wasn’t entirely operational. It includes a favorable prior-year reserve development of $164M. Last year’s 91.1% MLR also reflected the full first-half impact of the 2025 risk-adjustment true-up, making the comparison look especially strong. The bigger story is the guidance. Oscar raised its full-year operating income outlook to $500-700M from $250-450M while keeping revenue guidance unchanged at $18.7-19.0B. But the company has already generated about $1.09B of operating income in the first half, implying roughly a $400-600M operating loss in H2. That’s normal seasonality for ACA insurers, with MLR typically rising in the second half. Even so, the guidance implies an H2 MLR in the high-80s—around 88-90% by my calculations. The real story isn’t H1; it’s what management expects for the back half.

AXT: As hyperscalers transition to higher-speed transceiver modules, optical interconnect deployments are accelerating, creating a multi-year demand cycle. They also expect indium phosphide revenue to triple by year-end. Tower: Silicon photonics revenue is up 270% YoY and is on track to surpass the $1 billion run rate in Q4. They raised their 2028 outlook to $3.6 billion, are quadrupling their 300mm capacity in Japan, and have $1.3 billion in contracted business for 2027, with $290 million already received upfront. No one upstream in the supply chain is talking about demand weakness. Both companies are complaining about not being able to add capacity fast enough. $AAOI reports on Thursday. Are you still bearish?
